abstract: These are some thoughts inspired by Mike Reznikov’s recent paper “Designing RTL with C++HDL” [1]. C++HDL revisits a long lineage of executable C/C++ RTL, HDL generation, and cross-domain checking [9,13–17], but does so at a new moment: AI coding agents can now sit inside the fast edit-compile-test loop [3,4]. The central hypothesis is that this new computational actor may change the economics of an old architectural pattern by increasing trustworthy correction and design-space search per unit cost, while SystemVerilog remains the downstream compatibility and verification boundary. We propose experiments that attack the C++HDL/SystemVerilog semantic boundary, compare against a strong SystemVerilog + Verilator baseline [33], decompose representation from native-execution effects, test downstream PPA consequences, and separate migration from maintenance. The aim is not to claim that C++ has become a better HDL, but to define a falsifiable research program for asking whether an old architecture has acquired a new reason to matter.

blocks.text: Mike Reznikov’s “Designing RTL with C++HDL” is interesting precisely because its core architectural pattern is not new [1]. By 2000, C Level Design’s System Compiler could take C or C++ hardware descriptions into RTL Verilog or VHDL, while CycleC supplied a cycle-accurate coding style intended for fast native execution [9,22]. In 2002, a DAC paper described an RTL C/C++ flow with bit-accurate C as design entry, automatic HDL generation, and formal equivalence checking between the C-based RTL and generated Verilog [13].

blocks.text: Reflection needs a written acceptance contract. For the supported domain, say what must match—ports, state, widths and signedness, declared hierarchy or names, and cycle-level observable behavior—and say where differences such as two-state versus four-state semantics are allowed and checked. For downstream use, also say what names or source locations are expected to remain traceable. An unexplained observable mismatch inside that contract is a failure. Once understood, it becomes a permanent regression test.

blocks.text: That history also gives us a warning. C-like hardware flows did not displace Verilog and VHDL as mainstream RTL. Edwards’ 2005 survey identified concurrency and timing control as fundamental challenges, while contemporary reporting found C very useful for modeling and exploration but much less routine as a direct path into production RTL [24,25]. That is why the semantic attack, Verilator baseline, matched PPA budget, migration test, and maintenance test are central to the argument, not caveats.

blocks.text: An AI agent may change the value of an old architecture because it can exploit cheap feedback more aggressively than a human can. There are at least two plausible reasons. One is familiarity: frontier coding models have seen a great deal of C and C++, compilers, tests, build systems, debuggers, and software-development patterns. The other is feedback cost. An agent can make a small change, compile immediately, run a focused test, inspect a precise failure, instrument state, and try again. Which reason matters more is an experimental question.
